posts.title: Four team rituals that help new tools stick
posts.markdown:
New tools rarely fail because they are bad. They fail because nobody changed the meeting they were supposed to replace.

## The rituals

- **Show, don't tell:** ten minutes a week where someone demos a real piece of work.
- **One shared file:** a single place for experiments, so nobody works alone.
- **Office hours:** a standing slot for questions that feel too small to ask.
- **A retirement list:** what the new tool lets you stop doing.

Sample editorial copy. Replace it with your own.

posts.title: Three designers on speed, craft and expression
posts.markdown:
We asked three product designers how their work has changed in the past year. Their answers had little to do with software.

## On speed

"I sketch more and decide later. Fast is fine when nothing is final."

## On craft

"The details still take the time. They always will."

> Tools lowered the floor. The ceiling is still ours to raise.

This is placeholder interview copy for the magazine layout.

posts.title: How to make design system upkeep lighter
posts.markdown:
A design system is a garden. The work is not planting; it is weeding.

## Small habits

1. Audit one component a week instead of everything once a year.
2. Write the reason beside every rule.
3. Delete variants nobody has used in six months.

Teams that do this spend less time on big migrations because they never let the drift get big. Sample copy, ready to replace.
posts.excerpt: Less planting, more weeding: small habits that keep a system healthy.

posts.title: Workflow lab: staying in flow
posts.markdown:
Flow is fragile. One notification and it is gone for twenty minutes.

## What helped our readers

- Batching feedback into two windows a day.
- Keeping one file open per task.
- Writing the next step down before stopping.

None of this is new. What is new is how much harder it has become to protect. Placeholder copy.
posts.excerpt: Flow is fragile. Small defences that keep it intact.

posts.title: What it takes to build great products now
posts.markdown:
Ask ten leaders what has changed and you will hear ten answers. Ask what has stayed the same and they mostly agree: taste, judgement and the patience to say no.

## Three constants

- Know who it is for.
- Ship something small and real.
- Listen longer than feels comfortable.

Sample long-read copy for the magazine's feature slot.
posts.excerpt: Everything changed, except taste, judgement and the patience to say no.

posts.title: Source material: the references that taught us to look again
posts.markdown:
Every maker has a shelf of things they return to: a book, a poster, a chair. We asked a few of ours.

## The shelf

A worn type specimen, a children's picture book with impossible colours, and a photograph of a staircase taken on a holiday nobody remembers.

> Good references do not tell you what to make. They remind you how to look.

Placeholder copy for a recurring series.
